newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Islamist PM braces for censure motion.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Islamist PM braces for censure motion.

text.p: A confident Necmettin Erbakan faces a parliamentary censure vote on Wednesday, the first attempt by the secularist opposition to end his brief tenure as modern Turkey's only Islamist prime minister.

Erbakan and his pro-Western coalition partners, in power little more than 100 days, have the numbers on paper to head off a no-confidence vote, which parliamentary procedure mandates must follow any successful censure motion within a week.

"This vote will strengthen the government further. The government will be a lot stronger, it will continue on its way," the veteran leader of the Islam-based Welfare Party assured his parliamentary faction on Tuesday.
"We will serve until the year 2000," he said.

But the reverberations of Wednesday's debate are likely be felt long after the balloting, as opposition parties and dissident coalition members bear down to work out a viable alternative to the Islamist-led cabinet.
Turkey's mounting economic, political and foreign policy problems, ignored or even aggravated by the weak coalition, virtually ensure renewed challenges to Welfare's grip on power.
"I do not think parliament will even come to the point of taking up the confidence motion," political analyst Ali Bayramoglu told Reuters.
"The only power that could topple the current government is a sufficiently concrete and strong alternative, which is not yet on the stage," he said.
Consensus calculations show the opposition, itself badly split except on the need to remove the Islamists from power in officially secular, NATO-member Turkey, will come up just short.

Nominally, it needs 276 votes, a majority of the 550 seats, to guarantee victory. It can count on up to 269 MPs from its own ranks, plus a handful of dissidents from the True Path Party coalition ally. Welfare's iron discipline all but bars defections.
A banner headline in the liberal Yeni Yuzyil summed up the expected outcome: "A censure motion in vain."
However, there is no shortage of behind-the-scenes intrigue, with the opposition scheming to win over MPs from the True Path to a new government formula without the Islamists.

The opposition parties submitted separate censure motions, later combined, in protest at the prime minister's visit to Libya, where he received a lecture from leader Muammar Gaddafi on Turkey's treatment of its Kurdish minority.

This and other perceived slights to Turkish honour at the hands of Gaddafi -- as well as Washington's public rebuke for the visit to a state it says sponsors terrorism -- gave the opposition the opening they had sought to take on Erbakan.
It also follows a series of other foreign policy gaffes and high-profile U-turns by Erbakan, heartening his critics and sparking vague grumblings among the secularist armed forces.
Perhaps most fateful of all is a growing sense of economic chaos.

Inflation is running at 80 percent, with many analysts expecting a run at triple digits. Ballooning public deficits have sent domestic interest rates skyward, fueling the "rentier economy" Welfare had promised to eliminate.
The Turkish lira, meanwhile, devalues by the day against the dollar or mark.
Foreign investors, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund (IMF) are all warning of dire consequences if the government does not take matters in hand.
An IMF fact-finding team arrived in Turkey on Monday and any rescue effort would have the kind of tough conditions Erbakan has renounced throughout his career in politics.
"Even if the censure motion is surmounted, the IMF remains on the line," columnist Bilal Cetin said in Yeni Yuzyil.
"It seems a high probability the coalition will overcome the censure motion danger on October 16. But that is not the only danger awaiting," Cetin said. "There are more critical turns ahead."
